additions.reason: Prayer is the central subject of this entire Torah. The Rebbe's teaching is entirely about the quality and inner condition of prayer — what state the person must be in during prayer. תפלה is the dominant conceptual node of this Torah.
additions.source_quote: בִּשְׁעַת הַתְּפִלָּה, כָּל זְמַן שֶׁהָאָדָם שׁוֹמֵעַ עוֹד אָז אֵיזֶה אָדָם... הוּא לֹא טוֹב

additions.reason: Self-nullification (bitul) is the central positive teaching of this Torah. The person must nullify himself so completely during prayer that he does not feel even his own existence. Bitul is the primary quality described in the Torah's second paragraph.
additions.source_quote: מְחֻיָּב הָאָדָם לְבַטֵּל עַצְמוֹ כָּל־כָּךְ בִּשְׁעַת הַתְּפִלָּה, עַד שֶׁלֹּא יַרְגִּישׁ אֲפִלּוּ אֶת עַצְמוֹ כְּלָל בִּשְׁעַת תְּפִלָּתוֹ

additions.reason: The ideal state described in both paragraphs is that during prayer the person is alone with God — a state of exclusive unity. The formula 'אֵין שָׁם אֶלָּא אֲנִי וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְבַד' and 'אֵין כָּאן אֶלָּא הַמֶּלֶךְ בְּעַצְמוֹ' define the positive ideal of prayer as total exclusive presence with the Divine.
additions.source_quote: שֶׁיְּצַיֵּר בְּדַעְתּוֹ, שֶׁאֵין שָׁם אֶלָּא אֲנִי וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְבַד

additions.reason: The 'King's palace' is the metaphysical location where a person stands during prayer. This is cited from the LM2:55 teaching that is cross-referenced here. 'הָאָדָם עוֹמֵד בְּהֵיכַל הַמֶּלֶךְ' — standing in the King's palace defines the sacred dimension of the prayer space and explains why bitul is required.
additions.source_quote: כִּי אָז, בִּשְׁעַת הַתְּפִלָּה, הָאָדָם עוֹמֵד בְּהֵיכַל הַמֶּלֶךְ

additions.reason: The negative state described in the first paragraph — noticing and feeling the presence of another person during prayer — is the counterforce to proper prayer and bitul. This is the obstacle, the failure mode, the evil mirror to the state of exclusive divine presence.
additions.source_quote: כָּל זְמַן שֶׁהָאָדָם שׁוֹמֵעַ עוֹד אָז אֵיזֶה אָדָם, דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁשּׁוֹמֵעַ וּמַרְגִּישׁ שֶׁעוֹמֵד עוֹד אָדָם אֶחָד בִּשְׁעַת תְּפִלָּתוֹ, הוּא לֹא טוֹב

additions.reason: The person's own sense of self-existence (yeshuto) is the obstacle to complete bitul. The cited LM2:55 passage says explicitly 'מִי הוּא, הֲלֹא יֵשׁוּתוֹ נִתְבַּטֵּל' — his existence becomes nullified. The yeshut (self-existence, ego-sense) is what must be dissolved during prayer, making it the negative counterpart of the bitul package.
additions.source_quote: מִי הוּא, הֲלֹא יֵשׁוּתוֹ נִתְבַּטֵּל, וְאֵין כָּאן אֶלָּא הַמֶּלֶךְ בְּעַצְמוֹ

analysis_notes.notes: Torah LM2/103 is an extremely brief two-paragraph practical teaching with no explicit bechina language ('X הוא בחינת Y'). The Torah does not use the term 'בְּחִינַת' at all. It is a practical ethical note about the required inner state during prayer, cross-referencing the longer LM2:55 teaching. All concepts listed above are identified from close reading of the source text rather than from explicit bechina declarations. Two thematic packages emerge: Package 1 (good) = the ideal prayer state — bitul, exclusive divine presence, the King's palace; Package 2 (evil) = the obstacles — feeling other people, ego/yeshut. These form a clean good/evil mirror. Because the Torah itself contains no bechina edges, these additions represent the FULL package structure for this Torah, not supplements to an existing dataset.
